questions.question: For closed subsets $(\boldsymbol{E}_i)_{i = 1}^{\infty}$ of a metric space, what does the proposition say about $\bigcap_{i = 1}^{\infty}\boldsymbol{E}_i$?
options: It is closed.
It is always open but not closed.
It is closed only when the sets are finite.
It is never empty.

questions.question: For closed subsets $\boldsymbol{E}_1,\ldots,\boldsymbol{E}_k$, what does the proposition say about $\bigcup_{i = 1}^{k}\boldsymbol{E}_i$?
options: It is closed.
It is open but not closed.
It is closed only if $k = 1$.
It must equal $\boldsymbol{X}$.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}$, what is $\bigcap_{n = 1}^{\infty}[-\frac{1}{n},\frac{1}{n}]$?
options: $\varnothing$

questions.question: Which operation on closed sets is guaranteed to preserve closedness only in the finite case in the proposition?
options: Intersection
Complement
Union
Cartesian product

questions.question: Which stronger statement is true for closed sets?
options: Any union of closed sets is closed, even for uncountable families.
Only countable intersections of closed sets are closed.
Closed sets are preserved only under pairwise intersections.
Any intersection of closed sets is closed, even for uncountable families.

questions.question: A student claims that $\bigcup_{n = 1}^{\infty}[0,1-\frac{1}{n}]$ is closed because every set in the union is closed. What is the error?
options: The sets $[0,1-\frac{1}{n}]$ are not closed.
The theorem only guarantees finite unions of closed sets.
The union is actually $\mathbb{R}$.
Closedness is never preserved by unions, not even for two sets.

questions.question: Which set is an infinite union of closed sets that is not closed in $\mathbb{R}$?
options: $\mathbb{R}$

questions.question: Let $E_1,\dots,E_k$ be closed subsets of a metric space. A sequence $(x_n)$ in $E_1\cup\dots\cup E_k$ that converges to $x$ has a subsequence inside a single $E_j$, so $x\in E_j$. Why does this argument fail for an infinite union $\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}E_i$?
options: With infinitely many sets, the terms may be spread so that no single $E_i$ contains infinitely many of them.
With infinitely many sets, a subsequence may converge to a different limit than the full sequence.
With infinitely many sets, the individual $E_i$ are no longer guaranteed to be closed.
The argument does not fail: infinite unions of closed sets are also closed, by the same reasoning.

questions.question: In a metric space $(X,d)$, which statement about the whole space $X$ and the empty set $\varnothing$ is correct?
options: Both $X$ and $\varnothing$ are closed, and both are also open.
$X$ is closed but not open, and $\varnothing$ is open but not closed.
$X$ is closed and $\varnothing$ is open, and no set can be both.
Whether $X$ and $\varnothing$ are closed depends on the metric $d$.

questions.question: Let $F_1,F_2,F_3,\dots$ be closed subsets of $\mathbb{R}$. What can be said about $\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}F_n$?
options: It need not be closed, but it can be: $\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}[-n,n]=\mathbb{R}$ is closed, while $\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}[0,1-\tfrac{1}{n}]=[0,1)$ is not.
It is never closed: a union of infinitely many closed sets always misses a limit of its own points, as $\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}[0,1-\tfrac{1}{n}]=[0,1)$ does.
It is always closed: the proposition on unions of closed sets applies to any family, as $\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}[-n,n]=\mathbb{R}$ illustrates.
It is closed if and only if the sets are nested, $F_1\subseteq F_2\subseteq F_3\subseteq\cdots$.
